q: A force of 20 N acts at 60° to the positive x-axis. Its y-component is (sin 60° = √3/2):
x: Fy = F sin θ = 20 × √3/2 = 10√3 N. Using cos 60° by mistake gives 10 N, which is the x-component.

q: The scalar product of two non-zero vectors is zero when the angle between them is:
x: P · Q = PQ cos θ, and cos 90° = 0. At 0° and 180° the scalar product has its largest positive and negative values.

q: A force of 20 N acts at the end of a spanner 0.5 m long, at 30° to the spanner (sin 30° = 0.5). The magnitude of the torque, τ = r × F, is:
x: τ = rF sin θ = 0.5 × 20 × 0.5 = 5 N m. Using cos 30° gives 5√3 N m, and leaving out the sine gives 10 N m.

q: Vector P has rectangular components of 6 N along the x-axis and 8 N along the y-axis. The magnitude of vector P is:
x: P = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 N. Simply adding the components (14 N) ignores that they are perpendicular.

q: Two vectors of magnitudes 4 units and 5 units are inclined at 60° to each other. Their scalar product is (cos 60° = 0.5):
x: P · Q = PQ cos θ = 4 × 5 × 0.5 = 10. Using sin 60° instead of cos 60° gives 10√3, and forgetting the cosine gives 20.

q: A vector has an x-component of −5 units and a y-component of +5 units. Measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis, its direction is:
x: tan φ = 5/5 gives a reference angle of 45°. A negative x-component with a positive y-component places the vector in the second quadrant, so θ = 180° − 45° = 135°.

q: A force of 10 N pulls a box 4 m along the floor. The force makes 60° with the direction of motion (cos 60° = 0.5). The work done by the force is:
x: Work is the scalar product W = F · d = Fd cos θ = 10 × 4 × 0.5 = 20 J. Using sin 60° gives 20√3 J.

q: Three vectors have components (x, y): vector P (2, 3), vector Q (4, −7) and vector R (−3, 1). The magnitude of their resultant is:
x: Rx = 2 + 4 − 3 = 3 and Ry = 3 − 7 + 1 = −3, so R = √(3² + 3²) = 3√2 units. Adding the two sums (6) or taking only one of them (3) are common slips.

q: Vector P = 2î + 3ĵ and vector Q = 4î − 2ĵ. The scalar product P · Q is:
x: P · Q = PxQx + PyQy = (2)(4) + (3)(−2) = 8 − 6 = 2. The scalar product is a number, not a vector, and ignoring the minus sign gives 14.

q: A vector has equal x- and y-components of 5 N each. Its magnitude and its angle with the positive x-axis are:
x: Magnitude = √(5² + 5²) = 5√2 N, and tan θ = 5/5 = 1, so θ = 45°. Simply adding the components to get 10 N ignores that they are perpendicular.

q: Two vectors each of magnitude 2 units have a scalar product of 2. The angle between them is:
x: cos θ = (P · Q)/(PQ) = 2/(2 × 2) = 0.5, so θ = 60°. An angle of 90° would give a scalar product of zero.

q: A vector of magnitude F makes an angle θ with the positive x-axis. Its x-component is:
x: The x-component is the side of the right-angled triangle adjacent to θ, so Fx = F cos θ. F sin θ is the y-component.

q: Which statement about the scalar product of vectors P and Q is correct?
o: P · Q is a vector perpendicular to both P and Q
P · Q is greatest when P and Q are perpendicular
x: The scalar product is commutative because PQ cos θ does not depend on the order. It is a scalar, and it is zero, not greatest, when the vectors are perpendicular.

q: A vector has rectangular components Vx = −3 units and Vy = −3√3 units. Measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis, its direction is:
x: tan φ = 3√3/3 = √3, so the reference angle is 60°. Both components are negative, so the vector is in the third quadrant: θ = 180° + 60° = 240°.

q: The value of î · î + ĵ · k̂ is:
x: î · î = (1)(1) cos 0° = 1, and ĵ · k̂ = (1)(1) cos 90° = 0, so the sum is 1. A scalar product always gives a number, never a unit vector.

q: Which statement about the rectangular components of a vector is correct?
o: A rectangular component can be larger in magnitude than the vector itself
The two rectangular components of a vector make 60° with each other
The magnitude of a vector is never less than the magnitude of either of its rectangular components
A vector along the y-axis has a non-zero x-component
x: The vector is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle formed by its components, so it can never be shorter than either component. Rectangular components are always at 90°, and a vector along the y-axis has zero x-component.

q: The scalar product of two non-zero vectors is negative. The angle θ between them must satisfy:
x: P · Q = PQ cos θ is negative only when cos θ is negative, that is for angles greater than 90° up to 180°. At 90° it is zero and below 90° it is positive.

q: Three forces act on a body: 5 N along the positive x-axis, 2 N along the negative x-axis and 4 N along the positive y-axis. The magnitude of the resultant force is:
x: Rx = 5 − 2 = 3 N and Ry = 4 N, so R = √(3² + 4²) = 5 N. Simply adding all three magnitudes gives 11 N, and leaving out the 2 N force gives √(5² + 4²) = √41 N.

q: Vector P = 2î + 3ĵ and vector Q = 3î + 4ĵ. The projection (component) of vector P along the direction of vector Q is:
x: P · Q = 6 + 12 = 18 and |Q| = √(9 + 16) = 5, so the projection P cos θ = (P · Q)/|Q| = 18/5 = 3.6 units. 18 is the scalar product itself, not the projection.

q: The resultant of a set of coplanar vectors lies exactly along the x-axis. This means that:
o: The sum of the x-components of all the vectors is zero
Every vector in the set has zero y-component
The sum of the y-components of all the vectors is zero
The sum of the x-components equals the sum of the y-components
x: A resultant along the x-axis has Ry = ΣVy = 0. The individual vectors may still have y-components, as long as they cancel.

q: Vector P = 2î + 3ĵ and vector Q = 4î + ĵ form two adjacent sides of a parallelogram. The area of the parallelogram is:
x: Area = |P × Q| = |PxQy − PyQx| = |2 × 1 − 3 × 4| = |−10| = 10 square units. 11 is the scalar product P · Q, and 5 is the area of the triangle formed by P and Q.

q: The torque of a force about an axis is zero when:
o: The force is perpendicular to the position vector
The point where the force acts is far from the axis
The line of action of the force passes through the axis
x: τ = rF sin θ, or force × moment arm. If the line of action passes through the axis, the moment arm is zero, so the torque is zero. A force perpendicular to r gives the largest torque, not zero.

q: A force of 40 N is applied perpendicular to a door at a point 75 cm from the hinges. The torque about the hinge line is:
x: τ = rF = 0.75 m × 40 N = 30 N m. Leaving the distance in centimetres gives 3000, and dividing F by r gives about 53.

q: A 20 N force acts at the free end of a rod 0.8 m long, pivoted at its other end. The force makes 60° with the rod (sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 0.5). The torque about the pivot is:
x: τ = rF sin θ = 0.8 × 20 × √3/2 = 8√3 N m. Using cos 60° gives 8 N m, and leaving out the sine gives 16 N m.

q: A force F = (3î + 4ĵ) N acts at a point whose position vector from the origin is r = 2î m. The magnitude of the torque τ = r × F about the origin is:
x: τ = 2î × (3î + 4ĵ) = 6(î × î) + 8(î × ĵ) = 0 + 8k̂, so 8 N m. 6 is the scalar product r · F, and 10 N m is r × |F| as if F were perpendicular to r.

q: A force F = (2î − ĵ) N acts at a point with position vector r = (3î + 2ĵ) m. The torque τ = r × F about the origin is:
x: τ = (xFy − yFx)k̂ = (3 × (−1) − 2 × 2)k̂ = (−3 − 4)k̂ = −7k̂ N m, i.e. 7 N m along −z. Reversing the order (F × r) gives +z, a sign slip gives 1, and 4 is the scalar product r · F.

q: A wheel nut needs a torque of 60 N m to loosen it. Using a spanner 0.4 m long, with the force applied perpendicular to the spanner at its end, the force needed is:
x: F = τ/r = 60 ÷ 0.4 = 150 N. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 24 N; treating 0.4 m as 4 gives 15 N.

q: A force applied perpendicular to a spanner produces a certain torque. If the force is applied at half the distance from the nut, the force needed for the same torque is:
x: τ = rF; for τ to stay the same, halving r means F must double. Halving F would halve the torque further.

q: A uniform metre rod is pivoted at its 50 cm mark. A 10 N weight hangs at the 20 cm mark and a 5 N weight hangs at the 90 cm mark. The net torque on the rod about the pivot is:
o: 1 N m, turning the 0 cm end downward
1 N m, turning the 100 cm end downward
5 N m, turning the 0 cm end downward
x: 10 N × 0.30 m = 3 N m tends to lower the 0 cm end; 5 N × 0.40 m = 2 N m tends to lower the 100 cm end. The rod's weight acts at the pivot. Net torque = 3 − 2 = 1 N m toward the 0 cm end; adding the two gives 5 N m.

q: A uniform beam 2 m long and of weight 100 N is held horizontal, hinged at one end. The torque of its weight about the hinge is:
x: The weight of a uniform beam acts at its centre of gravity, 1 m from the hinge: τ = 100 N × 1 m = 100 N m. Using the full length 2 m gives 200 N m.

q: The first condition of equilibrium requires that, for the body:
o: The sum of the torques on it is zero
No force acts on it at all
The vector sum of all forces acting on it is zero
x: The first condition is ΣF = 0 (ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0), so there is no linear acceleration. The body may still move at constant velocity; zero torque is the second condition.

q: A paratrooper falls with a constant terminal velocity. He is in:
x: At terminal velocity the air resistance balances his weight, so the net force is zero while he moves: dynamic equilibrium. Static equilibrium needs the body to be at rest.

q: Three coplanar forces keep a ring in equilibrium. Two of them are 3 N due east and 4 N due north. The magnitude of the third force is:
x: The third force must cancel the resultant of the other two: √(3² + 4²) = 5 N, pointing south-west of the ring. 7 N simply adds the magnitudes, and 25 N forgets the square root.

q: A lamp of weight 20 N hangs at rest from two strings. Each string makes 60° with the vertical (cos 60° = 0.5, sin 60° = √3/2). The tension in each string is:
x: The vertical components balance the weight: 2T cos 60° = 20, so 2T × 0.5 = 20 and T = 20 N. Sharing the weight equally (10 N) ignores the angle; using sin 60° gives 20/√3 N.

q: A 30 N bob hangs from a string. A horizontal force F pulls it aside and holds it at rest with the string at 30° to the vertical (tan 30° = 1/√3, sin 30° = 0.5). The value of F is:
x: Vertically T cos 30° = 30 N and horizontally T sin 30° = F, so F = 30 tan 30° = 30/√3 = 10√3 N. 20√3 N is the tension T, 15 N uses W sin 30°, and 30√3 N uses tan 60°.

q: A see-saw is pivoted at its centre. A child weighing 300 N sits 2 m from the pivot. To balance it, a child weighing 400 N must sit on the other side at a distance of:
x: Second condition: 300 × 2 = 400 × d, so d = 600 ÷ 400 = 1.5 m. Inverting the ratio (400 × 2 ÷ 300) gives about 2.7 m; the heavier child must sit closer.

q: A uniform beam 4 m long and of weight 200 N rests horizontally on two supports, one at each end. A 400 N load is placed 1 m from the left end. The upward force of the left support is:
x: Torques about the right support: R_L × 4 = 400 × 3 + 200 × 2 = 1600, so R_L = 400 N. Check: R_R = 600 − 400 = 200 N. Sharing the total 600 N equally gives 300 N.

q: The net force on a rigid body is zero but the net torque on it is not zero. The body will:
o: Accelerate in a straight line without rotating
Move with constant velocity and constant angular velocity
Have an angular acceleration, while its centre of mass has no linear acceleration
x: The first condition is satisfied, so there is no linear acceleration, but the second condition (Στ = 0) is not, so the body's rotation speeds up or slows down. A couple is an example. Complete equilibrium needs both conditions.

q: A block of weight 40 N rests without moving on a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = √3/2). The friction force on the block is:
x: For equilibrium along the plane, friction balances the weight component down the slope: f = W sin 30° = 40 × 0.5 = 20 N. 20√3 N is W cos 30°, which equals the normal reaction.

q: A uniform rod 2 m long, weight 60 N, is hinged to a wall at one end and held horizontal by a vertical string tied 1.5 m from the hinge. A 30 N load hangs from the free end. The tension in the string is:
x: Torques about the hinge: T × 1.5 = 60 × 1 + 30 × 2 = 120, so T = 80 N (the hinge then supplies the remaining 10 N upward). 90 N just adds the weights, and taking the string at the rod's end (arm 2 m) gives 60 N.
